Martyrs, Morale, and Militarism: The Political Impact of Devastation and Slaughter Shizuka Inoue, David E. Weinstein, and Atsushi Yamagishi NBER Working Paper No. 33842 May 2025, Revised October 2026 JEL No. D7, H56, N45

## ABSTRACT

Do wars push the communities that suffer them left or right? We argue that the answer depends on the nature of the loss: communities respond differently to losing people and losing places. We show this using data from Japan’s WWII experience, where military deaths, civilian bombing deaths, and urban destruction varied across cities for reasons plausibly unrelated to their politics. Across sixtythree years of elections, cities that lost more soldiers voted disproportionately for Japan’s rightwing, pro-rearmament Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), while cities that suffered more physical destruction voted for left-wing, pacifist parties. Civilian bombing deaths move the vote in the same direction as military deaths. This pattern reconciles why WWI battle deaths pushed interwar Italian and German communities toward the right while building destruction in the Blitz pushed British cities toward the left. Survey, testimony, and organizational data indicate that deaths created “martyrs” whose commemoration benefited the right, whereas devastation durably lowered prowar “morale”. Our estimates imply that absent U.S. area bombing, the LDP would have won the two-thirds majority of Japan’s House of Representatives that is a necessary first step toward revising Japan’s pacifist constitution and rearming.

## 1 Introduction

Do wars push the communities that suﬀer them to the political left or to the right? The answer

matters beyond political history: strategies like “morale bombing” were premised on assumptions

about how devastation reshapes an enemy’s politics, and whether it stabilizes the postwar order by

pacifying the enemy or sows the seeds of future conﬂict. A century of evidence suggests that the

answer can go either way, and the literature has not resolved why. In Italy, Acemoglu et al. (2022)

show that municipalities with high World War I infantry casualty rates swung ﬁrst to the antiwar

Socialists in 1919 and then, within ﬁve years, delivered disproportionate support for Mussolini’s

Fascists. In Germany, De Juan et al. (2024) ﬁnd that counties that lost more of their soldiers voted

persistently for right-wing nationalist parties, including the Nazis, throughout the interwar period,

and Koenig (2023) shows that returning veterans shifted Weimar electorates durably from left to

right. Yet wartime suﬀering does not always feed the right. British cities that endured heavier

German bombing shifted toward Labour (Heldring et al., 2022), civilians on the front lines of

Colombia’s civil war were more willing than their countrymen to support peace and concessions

(Tellez, 2019), and a large literature ﬁnds that civilian victims of wartime violence become more

cooperative and altruistic, not more belligerent (Bauer et al., 2016; Blattman, 2009).

This paper argues that these seemingly contradictory ﬁndings are two sides of the same phe-

nomenon: communities respond in opposite ways to the loss of people and the loss of places.

We make use of novel Japanese WWII data covering nearly a century of elections to show that

deaths—whether of soldiers on distant battleﬁelds or of civilians in bombed cities—durably shifted

electoral constituencies toward Japan’s dominant right-wing party, the Liberal Democratic Party

(LDP), while the physical devastation of the urban landscape durably shifted constituencies toward

the parties of the left. We call the ﬁrst force the “martyr eﬀect”: the dead become sacred, and the

politics of honoring them belongs to the right. We call the second the “morale eﬀect,” after the

“morale bombing” that produced it: living amid ruins durably lowered communities’ identiﬁcation

with the political camp that had led the nation to war. We do not impose these labels on the data: in

over 1,500 wartime testimonies, accounts anchored in a soldier’s death disproportionately frame the

loss through sacriﬁce and honor, while accounts anchored in bombing disproportionately describe

the war as hopeless and futile. Because both forces operated simultaneously, within a single country,

a single conﬂict, and a single party system, Japan lets us separate them—and lets us test, rather than

assume, which dimension of the left–right divide wartime experience actually moved. The result

is that a war that ended eighty years ago continues to shape Japan’s political geography today—in

opposite directions, depending on what each community lost.

Our point of departure from this literature is to unbundle the eﬀects of wartime loss. Each of the

studies above uses variation arising from a single dimension of wartime experience, because each

setting supplied essentially only one source of variation: in WWI Italy and Germany, communities

lost their young men by the hundreds of thousands while their home cities stood untouched, and the

survivors ultimately moved right; in WWII Britain, German bombing damaged about two houses in

every seven while killing comparatively few civilians (Titmuss, 1950, Ch. XVI), and the survivors

moved left. Because deaths and devastation rarely vary independently within a single electorate,

existing evidence cannot tell us whether these opposite responses reﬂect diﬀerent treatments or

diﬀerent countries, wars, and party systems.

Japan provides the missing experiment because it suﬀered both forms of loss on an immense

scale: Japan had nearly as many military casualties in WWII as Germany and Italy had in World

War I combined (Hirota, 1992; Acemoglu et al., 2022; De Juan et al., 2024); U.S. air raids over

Japan killed over ﬁve times as many civilians as German air raids over Britain (Nakamura, ed, 1995;

Titmuss, 1950);1 and U.S. area bombing typically destroyed just over half the buildings in targeted

cities (Davis and Weinstein, 2002). Crucially, the two forms of loss struck diﬀerent places. Japan’s

hometown-based regiment system caused the draft cohorts of some cities to be decimated while

leaving others nearly untouched, and the only land battle on Japanese soil was in Okinawa, which is

excluded from our sample. Conditional on being targeted, civilian death rates varied substantially

politics by using an instrumental-variables strategy based on a city’s value as a bombing target,

which also corrects for measurement error in destruction. We can therefore estimate the diﬀerent

eﬀects of death and destruction in the same elections under the same party system, and we ﬁnd

within one country exactly the pattern the cross-country evidence hints at: wartime deaths, whether

military or civilian, pushed communities toward the right, while devastation pushed them toward

the left. The civilian-death eﬀect is less robust than the other two, however, because although there

is enormous variation across cities in the death rates for draft-age men, only two cities—Hiroshima

and Nagasaki—lost more than 2.5 percent of their residents to bombing. Moreover, greater urban

devastation predicts not only less LDP support, but also more support for the Japanese Communist

Party, the most stridently paciﬁst party in the opposition, even when we measure its support as a

share of all opposition votes.

Japanese postwar politics also allows us to interpret the left–right divide with unusual clarity.

Japan’s conservative LDP was explicitly formed to rearm Japan and strengthen security ties with the

U.S., and its opposition advocated left-wing, paciﬁst policies, so the country’s dominant political

cleavage mapped directly onto the questions the war had posed (Section 3.2). Moreover, the super-

majority required to revise the U.S.-imposed constitution banning rearmament kept that cleavage

salient for seventy-ﬁve years as right-wing politicians tried to win enough votes for revision. While

prior work (Ogasawara and Komura, 2022; Asai and Kambayashi, 2023) has shown that gender

ratios at the prefecture level reﬂect battle casualties, we improve on these measures by showing

that this variation can be used to construct estimates of casualty rates at the more disaggregated

municipal level. We follow recent work by Kimura (2023) showing that there was substantial

variation across cities within prefectures to build a municipal dataset with approximately 65 times

as many geographical units as earlier work based on Japan’s 47 prefectures, which we aggregate to

the 300 largest cities for our regressions—still leaving more than six times as many units. Indeed,

all of our identiﬁcation uses a full set of prefectural ﬁxed eﬀects, so our identiﬁcation arises from

variation across cities within prefectures. We assume that cities with high female-to-male ratios in

the cohorts of prime-age conscripts suﬀered high levels of military casualties, and we show that this

ratio is high in prefectures whose regiments were decimated and low in those whose regiments saw

little combat. We also show that the gender ratios of the adjacent, draft-ineligible cohorts cluster

near the natural ratio and do not predict LDP voting, so the draft-cohort ratio is not simply picking

up local diﬀerences in overall gender ratios.

We implement an approach that addresses many potential omitted variable biases. Our baseline

speciﬁcation explains a city’s right-wing vote share in a given postwar year by the war’s deaths

and devastation, conditioning on the same city’s right-wing vote share in 1928. A salient political

issue in that election was whether Japan should expand its navy. By controlling for votes for

the conservative Seiyukai party, a forerunner of the LDP that also supported expanding Japan’s

military, we control for a city’s inherent right-wing voting behavior. We augment this strategy by

also controlling for a variety of other potential confounding variables.

The political legacies of these wartime losses are also strikingly persistent. Consistent with

Voth (2021) and Ochsner and Roesel (2024),2 we ﬁnd that the martyr and morale eﬀects are present

in essentially every postwar election and show no attenuation over the entire 1958–1993 period,

even though most Japanese with direct experience of the war are no longer alive.3 The legacies

even survived the collapse of the postwar political system itself: after 1993, the LDP brieﬂy lost

power, the electoral system was overhauled, and the opposition was remade, yet both eﬀects, though

attenuated, remain clearly detectable in the new system through 2021.

Nor is this persistence a mystery: the martyr eﬀect is transmitted within families and reinforced

through conservative organizations for the war-bereaved, while the morale eﬀect is likely transmitted

through families and acquaintances but is also institutionalized in the peace education of children

born generations after the ﬁghting stopped. We use extensive data on Japanese attitudes and policies

to show the existence of these channels and explain both voting behavior and the persistence of

deaths in a positive light (e.g., as a sacriﬁce for the nation). Residents of prefectures that suﬀered

more military deaths were more likely to support expanding the military and the U.S. military

alliance and to prefer the LDP, even after controlling for their parents’ political preferences, and these

who lived through air raids were more likely to describe the war as futile, while residents of heavily

bombed prefectures were no more or less likely than others to view the American occupation as

positive. We also ﬁnd that more heavily bombed prefectures send a larger share of their school

children to Okinawa’s peace-education sites, where students are often instructed to make public

declarations to “hold a heart of peace” and to “pass it on to later generations.”4

We also conduct a simple counterfactual exercise to assess the magnitude of our point estimates.

We examine a scenario in which the U.S. decided not to use area bombing to destroy civilian targets

but instead just targeted the Japanese military. This counterfactual strategy would have reduced

the morale eﬀect in Japanese cities by leaving their structures intact and lowered the martyr eﬀect

arising from the killing of civilians. We ﬁnd that the reduced morale eﬀect dominates, and on

net the greater LDP support would have been large enough to enable the LDP to obtain more

than a two-thirds majority in the Diet’s House of Representatives. Since this has been one of the

major hurdles in achieving constitutional revision, our estimates suggest that the morale eﬀect is

suﬃciently large that it could explain why Japan has not revised its constitution to allow a military.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses the literature. Section 3 presents a

brief discussion of relevant Japanese politics over the last hundred years for readers unfamiliar

with Japan. Section 4 describes our data. Section 5 presents our main empirical results, assesses

their magnitudes, and summarizes our robustness checks, and Section 6 presents evidence on the

mechanisms behind them. Section 7 concludes.

## 2 Related Literature

In addition to the works already cited, our paper relates to several important strands in the literature.

First, our work is also related to work on how military actions aﬀect guerrilla activities. Kocher et

al. (2011) and Dell and Querubin (2018) examine the impact of bombing near civilian populations

and ﬁnd that it increases insurgent recruitment and activity. Lyall (2009) studied counterinsur-

gency operations in Chechnya, concluding that indiscriminate violence increased local support for

insurgents rather than deterring rebellion. Similarly, Jaeger and Paserman (2008) analyze Israeli

military actions and ﬁnd that targeted killings frequently led to retaliatory violence, reinforcing

militant group cohesion and increasing future attacks. Finally, Dell (2015) explores the unintended

consequences of militarized approaches to drug conﬂicts in Mexico, demonstrating that government

crackdowns on traﬃcking networks often lead to increased cartel violence.

Second, historians and political scientists disagree about the impact of military actions on enemy

morale, deﬁned as the willingness to ﬁght. Pollack (2002) provides evidence that overwhelming

military force can lower morale when it leads to the perception of inevitable defeat, as observed

in several Arab military conﬂicts where high casualties and sustained losses weakened combat

eﬀectiveness. Pape (1996) and Dower (1999) argue that bombing had small eﬀects on morale.

However, scholars such as Grayling (2007), Lyall (2009), and Jaeger and Paserman (2008) emphasize

the morale-hardening eﬀects of indiscriminate violence.

Third, a growing body of work on contemporary conﬂict ﬁnds that civilian exposure to lethal

violence pushes electorates rightward, echoing our martyr eﬀect. Studying Israel, Berrebi and

Klor (2008) show that localities suﬀering more terror fatalities shift toward the right-wing bloc,

an eﬀect they attribute to the right’s ownership of security policy, and Gould and Klor (2010)

likewise ﬁnd that local terror deaths raise right-wing vote shares. Getmansky and Zeitzoﬀ(2014)

ﬁnd that Israeli towns brought within rocket range vote two to six points more for the right. This

literature establishes that civilian victimization can move voters to the right, but it does not separate

the political eﬀect of killing people from that of destroying places: the ﬁrst two studies measure

<!-- Page 9 -->


only fatalities and contain no destruction channel, while the third bundles death, damage, and fear

into a single exposure indicator and concedes that it “is unable to adjudicate on whether the main

eﬀect of terrorism on political behavior operates through casualty aversion or through living under

threat” (Getmansky and Zeitzoﬀ, 2014). Because our setting varies deaths and physical destruction

separately, we can draw exactly this distinction, and we ﬁnd that the two move voters in opposite

directions. These settings also diﬀer from ours in that the adversary remains a live threat: a

rightward shift after an attack may there reﬂect a demand for future deterrence, whereas the eﬀects

we document persist for three-quarters of a century after the ﬁghting ended and the wartime enemy

became a close ally, so that they cannot be explained by prospective security concerns and instead

isolate the commemorative legacy of past violence.

Finally, our paper relates to work on the persistence and intergenerational transmission of

political attitudes, and in particular on the role of schooling in reproducing them. Voigtländer and

Voth (2015) show that Germans educated under the Nazi regime remained two to three times more

anti-Semitic than adjacent cohorts decades later, demonstrating that state schooling can durably

instill political beliefs. Consistent with this, Cantoni et al. (2017) ﬁnd that a curriculum reform

in China shifted students’ political attitudes, Clots-Figueras and Masella (2013) ﬁnd that bilingual

schooling raised Catalan national identity and support for nationalist parties, and Fouka (2020) shows

that prohibiting German-language instruction in U.S. schools after World War I durably shaped the

ethnic identiﬁcation of aﬀected children; Lott (1999) argues more broadly that governments invest

in public schooling partly to instill loyalty and shape political preferences. Our peace-education

results (Section 6) document the same channel operating in the opposite ideological direction:

schools in more heavily bombed communities transmit an antimilitarist outlook to children born

long after the war, helping explain why the morale eﬀect persists across generations.

## 3 Right-Wing Politics in Japan

In the postwar period, the LDP has been Japan’s right-of-center party, favoring more market-oriented

policies than its historical opponents, the Japan Socialist and Communist Parties, as well as their

8


<!-- Page 10 -->


more recent successors. Less well known outside Japan is that the clearest diﬀerence between the

LDP and its opposition concerns national defense. In this respect, Japan resembles the interwar

settings against which we compare it: in Italy and in Weimar Germany, whatever else divided

the parties, the political right was the pro-military pole. This section documents that Japanese

politics has been organized the same way for a century, with the conservative LDP and its prewar

predecessors on the pro-military side and the opposition on the paciﬁst side, and that voters have

understood it that way. Section 3.1 describes the 1928 baseline our design exploits, and Section 3.2

shows that the postwar LDP was assembled around rearmament and that the constitutional bar to

rearmament kept the issue salient throughout our sample period.

### 3.1 Militarism and Voting Before World War II

The ﬁrst election after the passage of the 1925 Universal Male Suﬀrage Act, which granted the vote

to adult men, centered on national defense issues. Tanaka Giichi, a former army general, became

president of the Rikken Seiyukai or “Friends of the Constitution Party” in 1925 and espoused pro-

military, imperialist attitudes. Tanaka advocated “popularizing national defense” and ﬁnding a way

for Japan to “break free from its insular position, become a continental state, and conﬁdently extend

its national power” (Duus, ed, 1988, pp. 94 and 275). The Seiyukai won the 1928 general election

on a platform of strong opposition to arms control. Because the 1928 contest centered heavily on

whether Japan should pursue military expansion, we use a city’s Seiyukai vote share as a prewar

benchmark for its inherited pro-military leaning and control throughout our analysis, separating

the eﬀect of wartime loss from a community’s inherited politics. We describe the benchmark as

pro-military rather than right-wing because the Seiyukai and LDP were not always conservative,

in the classical sense, on economic policy: both periodically favored expansionary budgets, loose

monetary policy, and rural public works (Metzler, 2006, pp. 67–68, 183).5

### 3.2 Militarism and the Liberal Democratic Party

For our purposes, the postwar LDP’s clearest distinguishing feature was its goals of rearmament

and constitutional revision, while its principal opponents deﬁned themselves by opposition to both.

This subsection documents that alignment and its stability over time, because it enables us to use a

city’s LDP vote share as a measure of its residents’ pro-military sentiment.

The lineage runs directly from the prewar party. After Japan’s defeat, the Seiyukai reorganized

itself into a pro-rearmament Liberal Party under Hatoyama Ichiro. From the ﬁrst general election

after the U.S. occupation ended, in October 1952, rearmament and revision of the U.S.-imposed

constitution banning Japan’s military were conspicuous in every campaign: Hatoyama favored

both, the Socialists opposed both, and Prime Minister Yoshida sought a middle ground of gradual

self-defense capacity without amendment (Ward, 1956, p. 50).6 In 1954, Hatoyama became Prime

Minister and formed the LDP the following year by bringing together Diet members who favored

rearmament. The party’s founding document made its position clear: “the primary focus of the

early occupation policy was on weakening our nation . . . We will establish self-defense forces

commensurate with national strength and circumstances under a collective security system, prepar-

ing for the withdrawal of foreign military forces stationed in Japan” (Liberal Democratic Party,

1955). Six decades later, Japan’s longest-serving Prime Minister, Abe Shinzo, described the party’s

origins the same way: “The Liberals and Democrats who formed the LDP wanted to create our

own constitution, and the merger of the two parties was done to achieve the two-thirds majority in

both houses that was needed for revision. Revising the constitution was the symbol of our regained

independence. It was for this that the Liberal Democratic Party was founded” (Council on Foreign

Relations, n.d.).

## 4 Data

We bring several novel datasets to bear on how wartime loss reshaped voting. Our analysis rests

on three exposure measures that map onto the paper’s central distinction between losing people and

losing places: military deaths and civilian bombing deaths—the loss of people, which we argue

produced the martyr eﬀect—and the destruction of the built environment—the loss of places, which

produced the morale eﬀect. We relate these to nearly a century of Japanese election results, which

let us measure a city’s voting before and after its soldiers, citizens, or structures were killed or

destroyed. Our death and destruction data are far more disaggregated than any used before, linking

wartime loss to electoral outcomes at the city level.7 Section 4.3 explains how the 1994 electoral

reform changes both the measure of LDP support and the periods over which we report results;

Section 4.4 describes how we construct the military-death measure and Section 4.5 the two air-raid

measures, which, though they arise from the same raids, may push voting in opposite directions.

### 4.3 The 1993–94 Institutional Break

The collapse of the “1955 System” in 1993–94 allows us to test whether the wartime political

legacies persisted after a major institutional change. The LDP had governed continuously since its

formation in 1955, with the Japan Socialist Party (JSP) as its principal opposition. The bursting of

Japan’s stock and land-price bubbles weakened the LDP and allowed a non-LDP coalition to take

oﬃce after the 1993 election, and the new government enacted a major electoral reform in 1994.

The reform changed both electoral competition and how we measure party support. Before 1994,

House of Representatives members were elected from multi-member districts under a single non-

transferable vote, which required candidates from the same party to compete against one another.

15


<!-- Page 17 -->


The reform replaced this system with a combination of single-member constituencies (SMCs) and

proportional representation constituencies (PRCs), so voters now cast one ballot for a constituency

candidate and another for a party. We therefore measure post-reform LDP support using the

proportional-representation vote, which most directly captures support for the party. PRC elections

account for about 38 percent of lower-house Diet members and are the most comparable post-reform

electoral counterpart to the party-level vote totals we construct for the pre-reform period.

The break also transformed party competition. The JSP ceased to be the LDP’s principal

opposition, opposition parties repeatedly reorganized, and the LDP returned to government through

new coalition arrangements: ﬁrst with the JSP and later with the more paciﬁst Clean Government

Party, which moderated the coalition’s constitutional-revision agenda (Samuels, 2004). Together,

these changes let us ask whether the legacies we document survive a wholesale institutional break,

and they are the reason we report results separately for the pre-reform (1958–1993) and post-reform

(1996–2021) periods throughout.

### 4.4 The Causes and Measurement of Military Fatalities

The value of the military-death exposure variable underlying the martyr eﬀect rests on two claims.

First, we argue that military logistics, rather than community characteristics, determined which

cities experienced high rates of military deaths. Second, we argue that city-level soldier death rates

varied suﬃciently to allow reliable imputation from the postwar census.

The Imperial Japanese Army (IJA) formed infantry regiments by recruiting men from the city

or county where they lived.11 Asai and Kambayashi (2023) argue that the allocation of regiments

to battleﬁelds was exogenous, meaning a regiment’s survival probability was unrelated to future

voting in its hometown. Because the IJA often did not know which islands would be attacked,

regiments sent to major battleﬁelds such as Iwo Jima and Okinawa had death rates close to 100

percent, while those stationed in Korea, Taiwan, or the Japanese mainland saw little to no ﬁghting.

The IJA deployed regiments based on training, experience, and battle fatigue, whereas American

### 5.2 Speciﬁcation and Identiﬁcation

While suggestive, these plots may not be compelling because they omit variables that could be cor-

related with urban destruction and military casualties. Similarly, soldiers in pro-military households

might have been more willing to sacriﬁce themselves for the country.20 It is therefore plausible that

in regions where Seiyukai support was particularly strong, young men were imbued with “military

ideology” and tended to ﬁght to the death and to vote for pro-military parties like the Seiyukai.

A diﬀerent issue with focusing on individual elections is that voters in particular elections

are inﬂuenced by idiosyncratic factors such as scandals, economic performance, and candidate

personalities. This was especially relevant before the 1994 electoral reform, when voters often had

to choose among two or more candidates from the same party. In these cases, LDP candidates

typically could not distinguish themselves from their opponents based on policy and needed to ﬁnd

other means (e.g., promising earmarked funds or agricultural subsidies) to win over voters. For

example, rural counties, which were typically not bombed, are also more likely to beneﬁt from farm

subsidies. This idiosyncratic variation may make it diﬃcult to see average patterns in the data,

which motivates us to pool our data across elections.

## 6 Mechanisms

The martyr and morale eﬀects rest on an interpretation—killing sacralizes the dead as “martyrs”

whose commemoration beneﬁts the political right, while the physical devastation of a city durably

causes its residents to identify with left-wing, dovish policies. This section presents direct evidence

for that interpretation, drawn from wartime testimony, contemporaneous opinion surveys, and data

on the organizations and school curricula that transmit wartime memory. First, we establish that

survivors’ memories and self-reported lessons from WWII diﬀer sharply depending on exposure to

morale bombing and military death, and we examine whether either experience also produces anti-

American sentiment. This shows that the martyr and morale eﬀects appear in personal memoirs,

and neither produces substantial anti-American sentiment. Second, we show that residents of

prefectures with more military deaths hold more pro-military attitudes, and that high-casualty cities

favor the party of rearmament rather than any party promising generous veterans’ beneﬁts. Third,

we show that voters in devastated cities disproportionately elect politicians who espouse paciﬁst

views, while voters in cities with high military and civilian casualty rates elect politicians who argue

for rearmament and constitutional revision. Fourth, we examine how families and local networks

transmit these political beliefs, and how this aﬀects participation in conservative war-bereaved

organizations or support for “peace education” in schools to transmit these views. To keep the main

text focused, we report the supporting regressions in Appendix A.6 and describe the underlying

datasets in Appendix A.1; here we summarize what they show.

The lessons of war: paciﬁsm, sacriﬁce, and anti-Americanism. We ﬁrst ask whether the

“morale” and “martyr” interpretations are visible in how survivors recollect the war. We built a

dataset of 1,509 “testimonies,” or personal recollections of the war, from a variety of newspapers

and other sources. Using a large-language-model coding of these accounts (Appendix A.1.3), we

classify each account by the experience it describes: area bombing, death of a soldier known to the

author, both, or neither.22 We also code the testimony to indicate whether it expresses the view

that the war was futile or hopeless, whether it frames a soldier’s death in positive terms (e.g., as

## 7 Conclusion

This paper set out to explain a puzzle: why do some communities emerge from war more right-

wing and others more left-wing? Our answer is that they respond diﬀerently to two kinds of loss.

Losing people—soldiers on distant battleﬁelds or civilians under the bombs—sacralizes the dead

and durably shifts a community toward the political right, a “martyr eﬀect” visible in the militarist

turn of high-casualty municipalities in interwar Italy and Germany and in the pro-rearmament vote

of postwar Japan. Losing places—the physical destruction of a city’s buildings—works in the

opposite direction, durably shifting communities toward the paciﬁst left, a “morale eﬀect” named

for the bombing strategy that produced it. Because Japan suﬀered both forms of loss on an immense

scale, and because they struck diﬀerent cities, we can separate them within a single country, war,

and party system—something no earlier setting allowed—and in doing so reconcile why battle

deaths pushed some electorates right while bombing pushed others left. These are not ﬂeeting

reactions. Both eﬀects appear in nearly every postwar election and show no attenuation across the

four decades of the pre-reform period, and both survive the wholesale reform of Japan’s electoral

system in 1994—the morale eﬀect still clearly signiﬁcant, the martyr eﬀect weakened but still

detectable. Nor is their persistence a mystery. Survivors’ own testimony and contemporaneous

surveys reveal the same divide the votes do—those exposed to death recall sacriﬁce and honor

<!-- Page 46 -->


and hold more pro-military attitudes, while those exposed to devastation recall futility and hold

more paciﬁst ones—and neither group is any more likely than the other to voice hostility toward

the United States. And these attitudes are actively reproduced: the martyr eﬀect passes through

families and conservative war-bereaved associations, while the morale eﬀect is institutionalized in

the peace education that sends children from more heavily bombed communities to study the war,

transmitting an antimilitarist outlook to generations born long after the ﬁghting stopped.

Our ﬁndings leave open questions we cannot fully resolve. The sharpest concerns are civilian

deaths: our point estimates suggest that killing civilians, like killing soldiers, produces a martyr

eﬀect, but while the point estimate is robust, statistical signiﬁcance is fragile. More broadly, whether

the opposing legacies of losing people and losing places generalize beyond Japan—to other wars,

other party systems, and other forms of devastation—is a question the comparative evidence we

have assembled invites but cannot settle.
